text: Northbridge's cluster started out running just catalog and checkout. Now the analytics team wants to run their own batch jobs on the same cluster, and nobody wants a naming collision or a stray command to reach across teams. A Namespace is how Kubernetes splits one physical cluster into multiple virtual ones.

Without Namespaces, every object lives in one flat space — two teams naming something "worker" collide, and a kubectl delete run in the wrong context has no boundary to stop it from hitting another team's objects. Namespaces give each team its own naming scope, and a natural place to attach quotas and RBAC rules.

Creating one is a single command: kubectl create namespace analytics. From there you target it with -n, or better, run kubectl config set-context with --namespace so your default context points at it and you stop typing -n on every command.

Most everyday objects are namespaced — Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets, Roles. A smaller set describe the cluster itself rather than one team's slice of it: Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, and ClusterRoles stay cluster-scoped, with no namespace at all.

A ResourceQuota then caps what a namespace can actually consume — CPU, memory, Pod count — protecting every other team sharing the cluster. Next up, lesson twenty-five: RBAC, which decides who's allowed to do what inside each namespace.
